Early-tenure record is activist: he launched Boundless Impact, a ten-year strategic plan; created SC Horizons, a multi-institutional agricultural innovation initiative; established the Clemson University Center for Invasive Species as a cross-college research and Extension effort; and expanded philanthropic engagement. He carries international affiliations with the International Livestock Research Institute and Queensland University of Technology. Warner College is CSU's natural resources college (forestry, fish/wildlife, ecosystem science, geosciences, human dimensions); the deanship carries no experiment-station or extension directorship, which at this 1862 land-grant sits with the College of Agricultural Sciences.

Academically he is a food process engineer - expertise in thermodynamics of phase-change heat transfer and moving-boundary problems - with 2,200+ citations, built over nearly 19 years at NC State (professor, later associate department head of Food, Bioprocessing and Nutrition Sciences) and nearly 7 years as head of Purdue's Department of Food Science. He runs a comparatively compact four-department college (animal and food sciences; applied economics and statistics; entomology and wildlife ecology; plant and soil sciences) and reports directly to the provost; the dean title here is not bundled with a separate experiment-station directorship. The department-head-to-industry-C-suite-to-dean path makes him unusually strong on industry partnerships and corporate fundraising.

raj khosla|washington state university.summary: Khosla was appointed May 14, 2025 and started September 1, 2025 as the Cashup Davis Family Endowed Dean of WSU's College of Agricultural, Human, and Natural Resource Sciences, succeeding acting dean Scot Hulbert. Scale is large and the numbers are on record: roughly 3,000 undergraduate and graduate students, 450-plus faculty, 600-plus staff, and more than $105 million in extramural research funding in 2024, with the college's teaching, research, Extension and outreach missions all under him (associate deans for Extension, research, and student success/academic programs report into the office). Scholarly standing is the headline here -- he is a globally recognized founder of the precision agriculture field, founding member and past president of the International Society of Precision Agriculture, and a Fellow of seven scientific societies including AAAS, the American Society of Agronomy, the Soil Science Society of America and the Crop Science Society of America. His policy reach is unusual for an ag dean: named a Jefferson Science Fellow by the National Academy of Sciences in 2012 and appointed Senior Science Advisor on Food Security to the U.S. Department of State, and inducted by NASA in 2011 to the U.S. Presidential Advisory Board on Positioning, Navigation and Timing, serving two two-year terms (2011-2015) on GPS policy. Career path is the classic land-grant lateral: 21 years on the Colorado State faculty (1999-2020, including the Monfort Professorship 2008-2010) building a globally recognized precision-ag research/teaching/extension program, then head of agronomy at Kansas State from January 2021, where he ran state-spanning research, education and Extension and co-led a $10M grant on artificial intelligence in agriculture.

kevin r. pond|west texas a&m university.summary: Pond has been dean of WTAMU's Paul Engler College of Agriculture and Natural Sciences since 2018 and is the most seasoned academic administrator in this batch: he spent 13 years on the North Carolina State faculty, 15 years as chair of animal and food sciences at Texas Tech, and seven years as head of animal sciences at Colorado State before the deanship -- a textbook department-head-to-dean land-grant ascent, though WTAMU itself is not a land-grant. He is an internationally recognized animal nutritionist, co-author of a leading animal nutrition textbook, holder of 14 patents, with nutrition, food safety and sustainability research across North America, Southeast Asia, South America and Northern Africa. No experiment-station or extension directorship attaches to the title. His defining current work is capital and industry-facing: WT broke ground November 10, 2025 on a $15 million research feedlot and education complex -- pitched as 'the feedyard of the future' with autonomous vehicles and robotics, 90 ten-head pens, 40 seventy-head pens, a feed mill and animal-processing facility -- assembled from a 2024 gift of 42.84 acres adjoining WT's Nance Ranch from ranchers Mike and Gary Kuhlman, a $2.1 million USDA grant for the education center, $2 million from the Engler Foundation and $1 million from Champion Feeders. That fundraising record, in the heart of Panhandle cattle country, is his strongest credential. He grew up raising sheep, swine and cattle in rural Ithaca, New York and runs a Texas ranch that has been in his family five generations.

jorge h. atiles|west virginia university.summary: Atiles holds the most heavily stacked JOINT title in this batch, and it is the whole point of the job: associate vice president and dean for Land-Grant Engagement, dean of the Davis College of Agriculture and Natural Resources, dean of WVU Extension and Engagement, and director of both WVU Extension and the West Virginia Agriculture and Forestry Experiment Station. He therefore runs the college, the state experiment station and the extension service simultaneously, delivering programs across all 55 West Virginia counties. The structure is new and he built it: WVU announced on January 18, 2024 that effective July 1, 2024 he would lead a newly created Division for Land-Grant Engagement merging three units -- WVU Extension, the Center for Community Engagement, and the renamed Davis College -- on a five-year contract with a three-year dean's review. He came to WVU in 2020 as dean of Extension and Engagement, so the 2024 consolidation was an expansion of an existing remit rather than an outside hire. HEADHUNTER NOTE: this is an extension-and-engagement career, not a production-agriculture or bench-science one -- his path ran associate dean for Extension and Outreach at the University of Georgia (until 2010), then associate dean for Extension and Engagement and professor of design, housing and merchandising at Oklahoma State, and his research is in workforce housing, water, energy, waste, indoor air quality and housing policy. He is also an unusual international profile for a land-grant dean, with a Dominican architecture degree and early career in the Dominican Republic's National Housing Bank.

ingrid c. \"indy\" burke|yale university.summary: Burke has been the Carl W. Knobloch, Jr. Dean of the Yale School of the Environment since 2016 and is the first woman to lead the school in its 125-year history. She is the most entrenched dean in this batch: on March 23, 2026 Yale reappointed her to a THIRD five-year term beginning July 1, 2026, with President Maurie McInnis and Provost Scott Strobel calling her 'an outstanding and transformative leader' and singling out research excellence, junior faculty mentorship and philanthropic fundraising -- treat her as very unlikely to move. Scholarly standing is top-tier: an ecosystem ecologist and biogeochemist working on carbon and nitrogen cycling in dryland ecosystems and how land use and climate variability alter them, with 180-plus peer-reviewed publications, more than $20 million in research grant support, and service on National Research Council committees, the EPA Science Advisory Board, and NSF and NASA advisory panels. Yale is private and not a land-grant, so there is no experiment-station or extension remit, but note her prior post: she came to Yale in 2016 from the University of Wyoming, where she was dean of the Haub School of Environment and Natural Resources, and she also taught at Colorado State -- so she has genuine western public land-grant experience. Her deanship has been defined by philanthropy and program launches: the Bekenstein Climate Leaders Program (2024), the Three Cairns Climate Program lowering barriers for emerging climate leaders from the Global South, five new online certificates including urban climate leadership and environmental data science, faculty expansion in forest ecology, water resource management and environmental justice, and YSE's physical expansion into the Prospect Street wing of Osborn Memorial Laboratories.

james soto antony|george mason universit.summary: Antony became Vice President for Academic Affairs and Provost at the University of San Diego effective March 1, 2026, moving directly from the provostship at George Mason University, where he served as Provost and Executive Vice President from July 2024 to March 2026, overseeing all colleges, schools, and academic support units at Virginia's largest research university. Before Mason he was Dean of Graduate Education and Postdoctoral Affairs at UC San Diego (Professor of Education Studies with a management courtesy appointment), and earlier spent nearly a decade at Harvard leading the higher education graduate program and co-directing its Management Development Program, held an Associate Provost role at Yale, and spent 17 years at the University of Washington as Professor of Education (with a Sociology appointment), including as Associate Vice Provost for Graduate Education and Associate Dean of the College of Education. His scholarship focuses on faculty development, leadership preparation for future college leaders, and data-informed decision-making in higher education.
